meta.expressionNote: Values are 0-100 illustrative scores derived from Human Protein Atlas single-cell RNA data, not raw experimental measurements.

organelles.name: Nucleus
organelles.blurb: Stores the cell's DNA, which holds the instructions for making every protein the cell needs.

organelles.name: Cytosol
organelles.blurb: The watery inside of the cell, where many proteins are made and glycolysis starts breaking down sugar for energy.

organelles.name: Plasma membrane
organelles.blurb: The cell's outer boundary, which controls what goes in and out and carries receptors that pick up signals.

organelles.name: Mitochondrion
organelles.blurb: Makes most of the cell's ATP energy, using oxygen and a chain of proteins called the electron transport chain.

organelles.name: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
organelles.blurb: A folded network of membranes where proteins for export or for membranes are made and folded, and lipids are built.

organelles.name: Golgi apparatus
organelles.blurb: Modifies, sorts and packages proteins arriving from the ER, then sends them on to where they are needed.

cellTypes.name: Neuron
cellTypes.blurb: Sends electrical signals through the body. Its branched dendrites collect messages, and its axon passes them on to many other cells.

cellTypes.name: Skeletal muscle cell
cellTypes.blurb: A long, cylindrical fiber with many nuclei that contracts to move the body. Oxidative fibers are packed with mitochondria to make lots of ATP.

cellTypes.name: Liver cell (hepatocyte)
cellTypes.blurb: The liver's main cell. It processes nutrients, toxins and wastes from the blood and makes bile, with plenty of mitochondria to power the work.
cellTypes.shapeNote: Shape simplified: real liver cells are many-sided (polygonal) and packed in plates.

cellTypes.name: Red blood cell
cellTypes.blurb: Carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. It has no mitochondria, so it makes its energy without oxygen and doesn't use up the oxygen it carries.

cellTypes.name: Pancreatic beta cell
cellTypes.blurb: Senses high blood sugar and releases insulin, a hormone that helps body cells take in glucose to use for energy or store for later.

genes.plainSummary: Quickly recharges ATP, the cell's energy currency, using a backup store called creatine phosphate. Busiest in muscle during sudden bursts of effort.
Makes skeletal actin, a protein that links up into thin threads inside muscle fibers. Those threads are needed for muscles to contract.
Builds a sodium channel, a tiny gate in a nerve cell's outer membrane. When it opens, sodium rushes in and helps fire an electrical signal.
Part of the machinery nerve cells use to release chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) at synapses, the junctions where nerve cells talk to each other.
Makes insulin, a hormone from pancreas beta cells. Insulin tells body cells to take sugar out of the blood, lowering blood sugar.
Makes glucokinase, an enzyme that adds a phosphate tag to glucose so cells can use or store it. Beta cells use it to sense sugar.
Makes albumin, a protein that liver cells release into the blood. There it carries fats, hormones and drugs and helps keep water inside blood vessels.

genes.fullName: cytochrome P450 family 3 subfamily A member 4
genes.plainSummary: Makes an enzyme, found mostly in liver and gut cells, that processes many of the medicines people take, plus some hormones and fats.
Makes beta-globin, one of the building blocks of hemoglobin. Hemoglobin fills red blood cells and carries oxygen from the lungs to the body.
Makes GLUT1, a doorway in the cell's outer membrane that lets glucose (sugar) in. It is the main way glucose reaches the brain.
Builds one part of ATP synthase, the machine in mitochondria that makes ATP, the cell's energy currency, using a flow of protons (hydrogen ions).
Helps switch on genes for making new mitochondria and controlling energy use. Especially active in muscle and liver.
Makes myoglobin, a protein in heart and skeletal muscle cells that stores oxygen and helps it spread through the cell.
A housekeeping gene: it is switched on in nearly every cell type. Its enzyme does one step of glycolysis, breaking down sugar for energy.

proteins.name: Creatine kinase M-type
proteins.job: Moves a phosphate between ATP and creatine (a small energy-storage molecule), letting the cell quickly rebuild ATP from its creatine phosphate reserve.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: In mice bred without it, muscles stay just as strong but can't do quick bursts of intense activity.

proteins.name: Actin, alpha skeletal muscle
proteins.job: Links into long thin filaments inside the muscle cell's contraction units (sarcomeres). These filaments are needed for the muscle fiber to contract.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Faulty actin can disrupt the thin threads, so muscles can't contract properly. This causes muscle weakness and floppiness (low muscle tone), sometimes severe from birth.

proteins.name: Sodium channel Nav1.2 (alpha subunit)
proteins.job: Forms a voltage-sensitive sodium channel in the neuron's outer membrane. When the voltage changes it opens, letting sodium ions flow in so the neuron can send an electrical signal.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Changes in this gate can make brain signals misfire. Babies may have seizures (bursts of uncontrolled brain activity); it is also linked to autism and developmental delays.

proteins.name: SNAP-25 (synaptosomal-associated protein 25)
proteins.job: Held on the inside of the cell membrane by fatty tails, it is a SNARE protein that helps control the release of neurotransmitters.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Changes in it can cause a severe childhood epilepsy: seizures (bursts of uncontrolled brain activity) that resist medicine, plus delays in learning, walking and development.

proteins.name: Insulin
proteins.job: Made as a longer precursor (proinsulin) that is processed and packed into storage granules, then released into the blood, where it signals cells to take up glucose.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Without working insulin, sugar builds up in the blood: diabetes. Some rare INS changes cause diabetes in babies under six months old; others cause diabetes in young people.

proteins.name: Glucokinase (hexokinase-4)
proteins.job: Adds a phosphate to glucose, the first step in burning it for energy or storing it as glycogen. It only works fast when glucose is plentiful, so it acts as a glucose sensor.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Weaker glucokinase means beta cells need more sugar before they release insulin, so blood sugar stays mildly high from birth (a diabetes called GCK-MODY), usually without symptoms.

proteins.name: Albumin
proteins.job: Made and packaged for release by liver cells, then floats in blood plasma, holding onto water, salts, fatty acids, hormones and drugs. Its main job is keeping water in the blood.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: People born with almost no albumin (very rare) usually have mild swelling, low blood pressure, tiredness and high blood fats. It is more dangerous for unborn babies and infants.

proteins.name: Cytochrome P450 3A4
proteins.job: Anchored in the ER membrane, it uses oxygen to chemically change (oxidize) many medicines, steroid hormones and other molecules, often making them less active.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: One rare change makes it overactive: it destroys vitamin D too fast. Children then develop rickets (soft, weak bones) early and respond poorly to vitamin D treatment.

proteins.name: Hemoglobin subunit beta (beta-globin)
proteins.job: Two beta-globin and two alpha-globin chains join to form hemoglobin. Each chain holds an iron-containing heme that grabs oxygen in the lungs and delivers it to tissues.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: The same tiny change in both copies causes sickle cell anemia: red blood cells bend into sickles, die early and block vessels. Other changes cause beta thalassemia (too little hemoglobin).

proteins.name: Glucose transporter GLUT1
proteins.job: Spans the cell's outer membrane and lets glucose pass through without spending energy, giving cells their basic sugar supply. At the blood-brain barrier it carries glucose into the brain.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Too little working GLUT1 starves the brain of its main fuel, glucose. This can cause seizures (bursts of uncontrolled brain activity), movement problems and developmental delay.

proteins.name: ATP synthase subunit alpha, mitochondrial
proteins.job: Forms part of the core of ATP synthase (Complex V) on the inner mitochondrial membrane, which uses the proton gradient built by the electron transport chain to make ATP from ADP.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Changes in it can starve cells of energy from birth. Babies may have poor growth, serious brain problems (encephalopathy) and lactic acid buildup; some die within weeks.

proteins.name: PGC-1alpha (PPARG coactivator 1-alpha)
proteins.job: A coactivator: in the nucleus it partners with nuclear receptors and other gene-control proteins to boost their activity, switching on genes for mitochondria and, in the liver, for making new glucose.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: In mice bred without it, mitochondria work less well and the mice are oddly hyperactive, with damage in a brain area that controls movement.

proteins.name: Myoglobin
proteins.job: Holds oxygen on an iron-containing heme group inside the muscle cell's cytoplasm (sarcoplasm), storing it and helping it spread to where it is used.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: One recurring change in myoglobin causes a muscle disease starting in adulthood: weakness near the body's center slowly spreads outward and can later affect breathing and the heart.

proteins.name: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH)
proteins.job: Carries out one step of glycolysis in the cytosol: it converts glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, a three-carbon piece of broken-down glucose, into 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
proteins.whatHappensIfBroken: Cells need GAPDH to stay alive, so scientists class it as an essential gene. UniProt, a major protein database, lists no human disease caused by changes in it.
